hints: Think of the overall photosynthesis equation as oxidation half-equation plus reduction half-equation, so subtract the water oxidation contribution to leave what must come from $\text{CO}_2$ reduction.
Scale half-equation 1 up to match the $6\text{O}_2$ in the overall equation, then balance C, H, O and charge with $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{e}^-$ on the left.
walkthrough:
See the overall as two halves added together**
You are told water is oxidised to $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{CO}_2$ is reduced to glucose. That means: overall = (oxidation of water) + (reduction of $\text{CO}_2$). If you remove the oxidation part from the overall, what is left must be the reduction part.

Scale the water oxidation to match the overall**
Half-equation 1 makes only $1\text{O}_2$: $$2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^-$$ The overall makes $6\text{O}_2$, so multiply by 6: $$12\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 6\text{O}_2 + 24\text{H}^+ + 24\text{e}^-$$

Subtract to isolate the reduction**
Overall: $$6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$$ Take away the scaled oxidation. The $6\text{O}_2$ cancels. You need $12\text{H}_2\text{O}$ on the left for oxidation but only have $6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, so bring $6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to the right, and bring $24\text{H}^+ + 24\text{e}^-$ to the left. This gives: $$6\text{CO}_2 + 24\text{H}^+ + 24\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check: 6 C, 24 H, 18 O and zero net charge on both sides.

hints: Recall that any $E^\ominus$ is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, so you need two half-cells joined together.
Think about what a gas half-cell needs when neither the oxidised nor reduced species is a metal: inert Pt electrode plus gas bubbled over it in contact with $\text{H}^+$ solution.
List what makes conditions standard for gases and ions in solution.
Remember how the two half-cells are electrically connected without mixing, and how the p.d. is measured with no current drawn.
walkthrough:
Start from the principle of Eominus**
A standard electrode potential is always the p.d. between that half-cell under standard conditions and the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), with $E^\ominus = 0.00\text{ V}$ by definition. So you must draw two beakers side by side.

Build the oxygen half-cell**
The couple is $\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Neither species conducts as a solid electrode, so use inert Pt foil to carry electrons. Bubble $\text{O}_2$(g) at 1 atm over the Pt through a gas inlet tube. Immerse it in $1.0\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ solution, e.g. $\text{HCl}$(aq), so $\text{O}_2$, $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ are all in contact at the Pt surface.

Build the reference hydrogen half-cell**
In the second beaker place Pt foil in $1.0\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ solution with $\text{H}_2$(g) at 1 atm bubbled over it. This is the SHE. Label gas pressure 1 atm and solution concentration $1.0\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ on both sides, and note temperature 298 K.

Complete the cell circuit correctly**
Join the two solutions with a salt bridge, e.g. filter paper soaked in $\text{KNO}_3$(aq), to allow ion flow without mixing. Join the two Pt electrodes with wire through a high resistance voltmeter to measure $E_{cell}$ with essentially zero current. Label salt bridge, voltmeter, Pt electrodes, gases and solutions clearly.

Final answer: Two half-cells connected by salt bridge and external voltmeter. Left: standard hydrogen electrode: Pt electrode in $1.0\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$ ($\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$), $\text{H}_2$(g) at 1 atm bubbled over Pt. Right: $\text{O}_2$ electrode: Pt electrode in $1.0\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$, $\text{O}_2$(g) at 1 atm bubbled over Pt. All at 298 K.

hints: Look up $E^\ominus$ for $\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in the Data Booklet and subtract the SHE value of $0.00\text{ V}$, then decide which half-cell gains electrons.
walkthrough:
Calculate and assign polarity**
From the Data Booklet, $E^\ominus(\text{O}_2/\text{H}_2\text{O}) = +1.23\text{ V}$ and $E^\ominus(\text{H}^+/\text{H}_2) = 0.00\text{ V}$. Then: $$E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{cathode} - E^\ominus_{anode} = +1.23 - 0.00 = +1.23\text{ V}$$ The more positive half-cell is reduced, so $\text{O}_2$ is reduced to $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ at the cathode. That makes the $\text{O}_2$ electrode the positive electrode.
Final answer: $E^\ominus_{cell} = (+1.23 - 0.00) = +1.23\text{ V}$; positive electrode is the $\text{O}_2$ half-cell (Pt with $\text{O}_2$).
